1184.title: The breaking of the vessels
1184.hook: the vessels couldn't hold the light and shattered, scattering sparks
1184.howItsDone: The breaking of the vessels is studied in Lurianic Kabbalah through Chaim Vital's writings, and Jewish teachers often bring it up when speaking about loss and brokenness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tzimtzum: in Luria's teaching, the Infinite drew in to leave room for a world. Your line: make room. Today, the next scene in that story.

Deep in Genesis there's a list that's easy to skim. "And these are the kings that reigned in the land of Edom, before there reigned any king over the children of Israel." Then name after name. And after every name but the last, the same short note: he died, and another reigned in his stead. Kabbalists slowed down at that list. Kings who rose and fell before anything could last. To them it sounded like a hint of something at the very beginning: a first world that couldn't hold.
screen: `A LIST OF KINGS.` → `HE REIGNED, AND HE DIED.` → `A WORLD THAT COULDN'T HOLD.`

segments.voice: Shevirat hakelim. The breaking of the vessels. It's the next scene in Luria's story, as Chaim Vital sets it down. First, the vessels. After the line of light entered the open space, it needed containers: vessels to hold it and give it shape. Second, the breaking. The light was too strong. Some of the vessels could not hold it, and they shattered. Their pieces fell, and with them fell sparks of the light, scattered downward. Kabbalists tied this to those kings of Edom: each one reigned, and each one died, a world that came and couldn't stay. Third, what's surprising. In this picture, the breaking happens before there are any people at all. No one's mistake sets it off. It sits inside the story of the beginning itself. Fourth, the sparks. The light didn't vanish when the vessels broke. It's still there, down among the shards, mixed in with ordinary things. Everything else in Luria's teaching turns on that. Some readers hear in it a word for a life: a marriage that came apart, a body that doesn't work the way it did, a plan that cracked down the middle. In Luria's picture, broken pieces aren't empty. They're where the light landed. Today, it's enough to know the shards are carrying something.
screen: `VESSELS TO HOLD THE LIGHT.` · `TOO STRONG: THEY SHATTERED.` · `BEFORE THERE WERE ANY PEOPLE.` · `SPARKS AMONG THE SHARDS.` · then, large: `BROKEN THINGS HOLD LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small thing in your life that's cracked: a chipped mug, a friendship that cooled, a habit you keep dropping, a part of your body that aches. Don't try to fix it; let it be what it is, and then gently look for any light still in it, a memory, something it taught you, someone it brought closer. If you find nothing, that's all right; simply rest beside it, without turning away.
Shevirat hakelim. The breaking of the vessels: in Luria's story, vessels that couldn't hold the light shattered, and sparks fell with the pieces. Today's word.
Your line: broken things hold light. In Luria's picture, the shards are where the light landed. Go gently.

1185.title: Gathering sparks
1185.hook: each good act lifts a spark back to its source
1185.howItsDone: In Hasidic communities, the idea of lifting sparks is taught as a reason to say blessings over food and to treat work, travel and ordinary objects with care, since each can hold something holy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the vessels couldn't hold the light, and sparks fell with the shards. Your line: broken things hold light. Today, what to do about the sparks.

In the book of Ruth, a widow walks into a barley field after the reapers have gone through. She isn't harvesting. She's gleaning: bending down, again and again, for the stalks that fell and were left behind. Slow work, done close to the ground, one stalk at a time. By evening she has enough to carry home to Naomi. Luria's followers gave every person a job that looks a lot like hers. The light fell. Now someone has to bend down and pick it up.
screen: `RUTH IN THE BARLEY FIELD.` → `BENDING FOR WHAT FELL.` → `SOMEONE HAS TO PICK IT UP.`

segments.voice: Gathering sparks. In Hebrew, the lifting of the sparks. First, where the sparks are. After the breaking, Luria's teaching says, sparks of holy light lie scattered, wrapped in husks. The Hebrew word is kelipot: shells or peels that hide the light the way a peel hides the fruit. Second, who gathers. In this picture, people do. A commandment kept, an act of kindness, a blessing said with care: each one frees a spark from its husk and lifts it back toward its source. For Luria's followers, the commandments weren't only rules. They were a way of gathering. Third, the ordinary places. Hasidic teachers carried this out into daily life and found sparks everywhere: in the food on a plate, in the tools of a trade, on the road to work. Eat with a blessing, deal honestly, speak kindly, and the thing in your hand is lifted. Some Hasidic stories say a person is led to a certain town, a certain meal, a certain stranger, because a spark there was waiting for them in particular. Fourth, the size of the job. Nobody gathers all of it. Each person has their own sparks, the teaching goes, and the work happens one at a time, like Ruth bending in the field. No grand gesture. A shard, picked up and set right. That's why today's line is so small. Not the whole world yet. One shard.

1186.title: Repairing the world
1186.hook: Luria's cosmic tikkun later became a word for social justice
1186.howItsDone: Tikkun olam is spoken of in Jewish schools, synagogues and community groups as a reason for charity and justice work, while the phrase also stays in the Aleinu prayer said in services.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gathering sparks: each good act frees one from its husk and lifts it toward its source. Your line: repair a shard. Today, a phrase with a long road behind it.

Near the end of the service in the Jewish prayer book stands a prayer called Aleinu. Toward its close is a hope, and in Hebrew it reads l'taken olam b'malchut Shaddai: to set the world right under the kingdom of the Almighty. Today, that short phrase, tikkun olam, turns up on synagogue banners, on school volunteer days, on the side of a food drive. How did a line from a prayer, and a teaching about broken vessels, end up on a sign by the canned goods? It has quite a road behind it.
screen: `A LINE IN THE ALEINU.` → `ON A FOOD-DRIVE SIGN.` → `HOW DID IT GET THERE?`

segments.voice: Repairing the world. Tikkun olam. Follow the phrase four steps down its road. First, the law. In the Mishnah, the rabbis make certain rulings, they say, for the sake of tikkun ha'olam. Rules about how a divorce document is written, so no one is trapped by a careless name. A rule that captives are not ransomed for more than they're worth; one reason later readers give is that kidnapping shouldn't become a business. Here, repairing the world means keeping society fair and in working order. Second, the prayer. In the Aleinu, the phrase lifts its eyes. It becomes a hope for the whole world, set right under God's kingship. Not a rule anymore, a horizon. Third, Luria. In his teaching, tikkun becomes cosmic. The vessels broke; the sparks fell. Every commandment and every kind act gathers a spark and mends a piece of what shattered. Repair isn't only for society now. It's for creation itself, and every person has a share in it. Fourth, today. In more recent times, tikkun olam has become a common name for work for justice: feeding the hungry, caring for the earth, standing up for people pushed aside. Some teachers welcome that wide use. Others ask that it keep its roots in the commandments and in prayer. Both are Jewish voices, and both are part of its story. Read this way, what ties the four together is the sense that the world is not finished, and that people's hands belong in the finishing. A rule, a prayer, a spark, a sandwich handed across a table.
screen: `THE MISHNAH: A FAIR SOCIETY.` · `THE ALEINU: A HOPE.` · `LURIA: MENDING CREATION.` · `TODAY: WORK FOR JUSTICE.` · then, large: `REPAIR THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small thing you did recently: holding a door, paying someone on time, calling a parent. 1187.title: Souls return
1187.hook: many kabbalists taught reincarnation; not all Jews hold this view
1187.howItsDone: Gilgul is taught in Kabbalah and Hasidic thought, especially through Chaim Vital's Sha'ar ha-Gilgulim; other Jews focus instead on the soul's return to God, the world to come, and the resurrection of the dead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, repairing the world: a phrase that ran from the Mishnah to a food-drive sign. Your line: repair the world. Today, an old question about the soul.

"One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh; and the earth abideth for ever." That's Ecclesiastes, watching the parade go by. People arrive, people leave, the ground stays put. But the line leaves a question hanging. The earth abides. What about the soul that walked on it for one generation? Jewish tradition holds more than one answer to that, side by side. Today's word belongs to the kabbalists, and it isn't the only Jewish answer.
screen: `ONE GENERATION PASSES.` → `THE EARTH ABIDES.` → `AND THE SOUL?`

segments.voice: Gilgul. In full, gilgul neshamot, often put into English as the cycling of souls. First, what it says. Kabbalists taught that a soul can come back to this world in another life, in another body. The Zohar speaks of it, and Chaim Vital gathered Luria's teachings on it into a book called Sha'ar ha-Gilgulim, the Gate of Reincarnations. Second, why a soul returns. The reason these teachers give is repair, tikkun, the thread from the last few days. A soul comes back to finish a commandment it missed, to mend a wrong, to complete its share of gathering the sparks. Not a punishment so much as unfinished work. Third, the other voices. Not all Jews hold this view. The Torah doesn't spell it out. Saadia Gaon, a medieval Jewish philosopher, argued against it, and other thinkers set it aside. Jewish tradition also speaks, in its own words, of the soul returning to God, of the world to come, and of the resurrection of the dead. Ecclesiastes says simply that the spirit returneth unto God who gave it. These views live in the same tradition, and people who hold them pray side by side. Fourth, what they share. Whether a soul returns, rests with God, or waits for the world to come, none of these answers treats a life as a sealed box. What a person does spills past them: a name given in memory, a kindness taught to a child, a promise kept by a grandchild. Some readers hear gilgul as that same idea, told in the language of souls.
screen: `A SOUL CAN RETURN.` · `TO FINISH ITS REPAIR.` · `NOT ALL JEWS HOLD THIS.` · `A LIFE IS NOT A SEALED BOX.` · then, large: `SOULS CONTINUE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who has died whose ways still show up in you: a phrase, a recipe, the way you fold a towel, a kindness; if no one comes to mind, choose a teacher or an author. Hold that thread for a while, then turn it forward: what of yours might carry on after you? No need to decide anything; just notice the threads, running back and running forward.
Gilgul. The return of a soul to another life, taught by kabbalists as a way to finish its repair, and not held by all Jews. Today's word.

1188.title: Intentions in prayer
1188.hook: mystical meditations attached to the words of prayer
1188.howItsDone: Kavanah, directing the heart, is taught as part of Jewish prayer; in kabbalistic circles, some pray from prayer books that print Lurianic meditations beside the words, and some say a line beginning l'shem yichud before a commandment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gilgul: the kabbalists' teaching that a soul can return to finish its repair. Your line: souls continue. Today, where the heart points while the mouth prays.

The Mishnah remembers a group it calls the pious ones of old. Before they prayed, it says, they would wait an hour, just to direct their hearts toward God. A whole hour of getting ready, before the first word. Some mornings, finding the right page is as far as anyone gets. But the question they were answering is an old and practical one. When the mouth says the words, where is the heart pointed? Later kabbalists answered it in fine detail.
screen: `THE PIOUS ONES OF OLD.` → `AN HOUR BEFORE THE FIRST WORD.` → `WHERE IS THE HEART POINTED?`

segments.voice: Kavanot. The plural of kavanah: intention, the direction of the heart. First, the old rule. The Mishnah imagines someone reading the Torah aloud who reaches the passage of the Shema just as the time comes to say it. Does it count as their Shema? If they directed their heart, the Mishnah says, they have fulfilled it. Intention is what turns reading into prayer. Second, the kabbalists' kavanot. Luria and his students taught particular meditations to hold while saying the words of the prayers: divine names, the sefirot, the joining of one to another. A single word in the prayer book could carry a whole map. Some prayer books print these meditations beside the words, for those who pray with them. Third, a short doorway. Before doing a commandment, some Jews say a line that begins l'shem yichud, for the sake of the unification, naming the Holy One and the Shechinah, the indwelling presence from earlier in this stretch. In the kabbalists' language, the act joins what had been apart. Fourth, the Hasidic turn. Some Hasidic teachers taught a simpler kavanah for people who would never learn the full meditations: pray with your whole heart, cling to the words, let them carry you. Every one of these keeps the words the same. What changes is where the heart is pointed. Two people can say the same blessing over the same bread. One is reciting it. The other means it.
screen: `INTENTION MAKES READING PRAYER.` · `MEDITATIONS ON THE WORDS.` · `FOR THE SAKE OF UNIFICATION.` · `THE SIMPLER WAY: THE WHOLE HEART.` · then, large: `INTEND.`

segments.voice: If you say blessings, choose one you know well, over bread, over water, on waking; if you don't, choose a simple thank-you you say often. Before the words, pause and ask what exactly you're pointing them toward: this glass of water, the person who cooked, the body that's thirsty, God, if you pray. Then say the words slowly, with that one intention riding on them, and rest in the quiet after.
Kavanot. Intentions: meditations attached to the words of prayer, so the heart is pointed somewhere while the mouth speaks. Today's word.
Your line: intend. The same words can be recited by the mouth, or meant by the heart. Rest well.

1189.title: Cautions
1189.hook: teachers warn against magic, charms sold for money, and study without grounding
1189.howItsDone: Jewish mysticism is traditionally studied within a framework of Torah, Jewish law and community, and teachers in the tradition warn students away from amulets, paid blessings and the use of holy names as magic.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kavanot: intentions attached to the words of prayer. Your line: intend. Today, the tradition's own warnings.

A charm in a shop window, with Hebrew letters stamped on it and a little card promising luck. A course online that says it will unlock the secret names in a weekend, card details please. The word Kabbalah can end up on a price tag. But some of the sharpest warnings about this kind of thing don't come from critics outside. They come from inside the tradition, from the Torah, the Mishnah and its own teachers.
screen: `A CHARM WITH A PRICE TAG.` → `SECRETS IN A WEEKEND.` → `THE WARNINGS COME FROM INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Cautions. First, the Torah's own line. Deuteronomy names practices that are not to be found among the people: divining, reading omens, sorcery, casting spells, asking the dead. Then it sums up what it wants instead, in a short phrase that begins tamim tihyeh: be whole-hearted with the LORD your God. Not clever, not powerful. Whole. Second, the crown and the spade. In Pirkei Avot, Rabbi Tzadok says not to make the Torah a crown to make yourself great, nor a spade to dig with. Holy learning isn't a tool for status or a way to dig up money. Charms sold for profit fall right under that warning. Third, words as cures. Maimonides objected to people who whisper over a wound and read a verse of Torah to heal it. The words of Torah, he wrote, are healing for the soul, not medicine for the body. And within Kabbalah itself, teachers drew a line between learning about God and trying to use holy names to change things in the world, and warned students away from the second. Fourth, grounding. Mystical ideas without a floor under them can drift: into fear, into pride, into the feeling of having secret knowledge others don't. The tradition's answer is a floor of plain learning, a community, and a teacher whose life matches their words. So study carefully looks like ordinary questions. Who taught this person? What do they ask of me? Does this teaching send me back toward kindness, honest work and the commandments, or toward my wallet? A careful student isn't a suspicious one. They just check the ground before they stand on it.
screen: `BE WHOLE-HEARTED, NOT POWERFUL.` · `NOT A CROWN, NOT A SPADE.` · `VERSES HEAL THE SOUL.` · `A FLOOR UNDER THE MYSTERY.` · then, large: `STUDY CAREFULLY.`

1190.title: No place without God
1190.hook: Hasidic teaching: no place is empty of God
1190.howItsDone: Hasidic teachers repeat the line that no place is empty of God as a reason to serve God in ordinary life, at work, at meals and on the road, and not only in the synagogue or study house.

segments.voice: Yesterday, cautions: no magic, no selling holy things, no study without ground beneath it. Your line: study carefully. Today, a man asleep on a stone.

A man is running from his brother. Night falls somewhere in the open, and he lies down on the ground with a stone under his head. Nowhere special. Just the spot where the sun went down. He dreams of a ladder, with angels going up and down it, and when he wakes he says: "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not." The place hadn't changed overnight. Jacob had. Hasidic teachers made much of that surprise.
screen: `A STONE FOR A PILLOW.` → `A LADDER IN A DREAM.` → `AND I KNEW IT NOT.`

segments.voice: No place without God. First, the prophet. Isaiah sees the angels calling to one another: "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of His glory." Not the Temple only. The whole earth. Second, the kabbalists' line. The Tikkunei Zohar, a work in the Zohar's family, says it in Aramaic: leit atar panui minei, there is no place empty of Him. The rabbis even give God a name that means the Place, HaMakom. And remember tzimtzum, a week ago: if God drew in to make room for a world, is that room empty? The Hasidic reading answers no. The hiding is real. The emptiness isn't. Third, the street. Hasidic teachers carried the line out of the study house into kitchens, markets and workshops. If no place is empty of God, then the bus stop, the laundry pile and the waiting room are not outside holiness. They're places where it's hidden. Fourth, the hard places. A line like this is easy at sunset and harder in a bad week. But notice where Jacob found it: on a stone pillow, running for his life. There is nowhere the sparks fell where God is absent.
screen: `THE WHOLE EARTH IS FULL.` · `NO PLACE IS EMPTY OF HIM.` · `THE BUS STOP AND THE LAUNDRY.` · `EVEN ON A STONE PILLOW.` · then, large: `NO PLACE WITHOUT HIM.`

segments.voice: Look at the place you're in right now, exactly as it is, the chair, the light, the clutter, and let your eyes move slowly from one ordinary thing to the next, holding one simple thought: even here. If you pray, you can say Jacob's words quietly: surely the LORD is in this place. If you don't, just stay with the place, and let it be enough.
No place without God. The Hasidic teaching, drawn from the Tikkunei Zohar, that no place is empty of Him. Today's words.
Your line: no place without him. The sink and the sidewalk aren't outside holiness. Back tomorrow, same hill.
